NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern for item missingness in the analytical sample (n = 103 across Tables 1, 5, and 6), though initial field refusal/non-response rates are not reported (Can't tell), Table 3 has an unexplained 1-person discrepancy in WUSC sex counts (91 male + 11 female = 102 vs. n = 103), and 5-10% missing historical records at four meteorological stations were imputed.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk: no confounding factors were controlled for in the regression models (Tables 5 and 6 report separate unadjusted bivariate linear regressions), despite substantial cross-regional variation across three distinct physiographic zones, differing scheme ages (2011-2021) and sizes, and respondents noting non-climatic drivers such as reckless local road construction and delayed maintenance.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak: community-managed Water Users and Sanitation Committees (WUSCs) and Ministry of Water Supply (MoWS 2016) functionality tiers frame the sample, and an institutional component (18 out of 100 FIETS points) is scored via WUSC interviews, but statutory mandates, formal WUSC registration/bylaws, tariff rules, and regulatory compliance are not doctrinally defined or disaggregated in the main text (relegated to Supplementary Material 2).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk: in the system-level analytical regressions (n = 103), climatic exposures, hazard mediators/moderators, and WASH impact outcomes were all measured simultaneously via unblinded retrospective perceptions (over a 25-year recall window) from the same WUSC/caretaker respondents, producing severe recall bias and common-method variance (reflected in bivariate R2 values of 0.80-0.93 in Table 5). Municipal-level DHM weather station trends (1994-2024) corroborate regional warming/drying only at an aggregate station level.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate: tap-stand functionality (3,896 taps) applied MoWS (2016) categorical thresholds (Table 2) and sustainability applied an expert-adapted 43-indicator FIETS index (Cronbach's alpha = 0.75), but source depletion, drying up, water turbidity, flow sufficiency, supply hours, and sanitation status were measured solely via caretaker and WUSC self-reports without physical flow metering, water-quality testing, or independent technical inspection, and functionality was double-counted inside the re-weighted FIETS score.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no study protocol or pre-analysis plan is mentioned; Tables 5 and 6 omit several predictor-outcome combinations (marked 'X') without clarifying whether they were excluded a priori or after testing; exact regression item scales are placed in Supplementary Material 1; and Table 3 contains a minor arithmetic discrepancy in WUSC respondent sex counts (91 + 11 = 102 vs. 103).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: three provinces/districts/municipalities were purposively chosen based on climatic zone and secondary data availability, and sampling was restricted to NEWAH/NWASH-documented schemes built in 2011-2021 (excluding older or undocumented systems). Proportional random sampling of 103 of 138 eligible systems strengthens within-municipality scheme representativeness, but purposive respondent selection (age >= 40 years, residency >= 25 years) yielded a heavily male sample (88% of WUSCs and 97% of caretakers) and participation/refusal rates were not reported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion criteria were clearly specified at both the system and respondent levels: community-managed WASH systems located in the three selected municipalities and constructed during the 10-year window from 2011 to 2021 (population N = 138, sample n = 103), and one WUSC representative plus one caretaker per sampled system meeting purposive thresholds of age >= 40 years and continuous community residency >= 25 years.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 5, Section 2.3.2 (Table 1); PDF Page 6, Section 3.1 (Table 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The three study municipalities (Tinpatan RM in Sindhuli, Badigad RM in Baglung, and Chandannath Municipality in Jumla) are described in detail with household counts, basic WASH coverage, elevation ranges, temperature ranges, annual rainfall, and DEM maps (Figure 1, Table 1). Respondent demographics (sex, mean age, mean residency duration, and WUSC education levels) and field collection dates (January-February 2024) are also clearly reported, notwithstanding a 1-respondent sum discrepancy in Table 3 WUSC sex counts (91 + 11 = 102 vs. 103).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: In the cross-sectional regression models (n = 103; Tables 5 and 6), the independent variables (less rainfall, intense rainfall, high temperature) and hazard variables (drought, flood, landslide) were measured via respondents' retrospective 25-year perceptions rather than objective, scheme-specific meteorological or hazard measurements. While 30-year DHM weather station series (one station per municipality, with 5-10% missing values imputed via normal-ratio and mean-substitution methods) descriptively corroborated regional trends, subjective long-term recall used as the regression exposure is highly susceptible to recall and common-method bias, and psychometric properties/scales for the climate perception items are not reported in the main text.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4, Sections 2.2-2.3; PDF Page 5, Sections 2.3.1 & 2.3.3; PDF Pages 7-9, Sections 3.2-3.3 & Tables 4-5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the study referenced official NEWAH/NWASH scheme registries and adopted Ministry of Water Supply (MoWS 2016) functionality tiers (Table 2) and Malik et al. (2016) FIETS sustainability tiers, actual assessment of system condition—including spring/stream depletion, tap-stand flow sufficiency, supply hours, and seasonal turbidity—relied on caretaker and WUSC interviews rather than objective physical discharge measurements, metered supply logs, or laboratory/instrument water quality testing.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4, Section 2.2; PDF Pages 5-6, Section 2.3.4 & Table 2; PDF Pages 9-10, Section 3.4.1

domain_ratings.justification: The conceptual framework and analytical design (Figure 2, Sections 2.3-2.4) did not systematically identify confounding variables that could jointly affect perceived hazards and WASH degradation (such as physiographic zone/elevation, scheme age within 2011-2021, user population/tap count, initial construction quality, or O&M governance). Although localized river/altitude proximity, delayed maintenance, and reckless local road construction are mentioned narratively in the Results and Discussion, they were not treated as confounders in the study design.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4, Section 2.3 & Figure 2; PDF Page 6, Section 2.4; PDF Page 8, Section 3.3; PDF Page 10, Section 3.4.1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No design-based or statistical strategies (such as multivariable regression adjustment, municipality/physiographic fixed effects, stratification, or matching) were stated or applied to control for confounding. All reported regressions in Tables 5 and 6 are unadjusted single-predictor linear regressions.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 5, Section 2.3.3; PDF Page 6, Section 2.4; PDF Pages 9-10, Tables 5 & 6

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: While the questionnaire underwent expert panel review and pilot testing in 20 systems and the 43-item FIETS index achieved acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.75), primary WASH outcomes—source depletion, drying up, water quality deterioration (Table 6), tap-stand functionality, and sustainability—were measured exclusively via unblinded WUSC and caretaker self-reports without physical hydrological gauging or water-quality testing, creating severe same-source bias when regressed against perceived hazards. Moreover, re-weighting Technical (30%) and Environmental (22%) components incorporated functionality directly into the sustainability score.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6, Sections 2.3.1 & 2.3.4 & Table 2; PDF Pages 9-11, Sections 3.4.1-3.4.2 & Table 6

domain_ratings.justification: Statistical analysis was inappropriate in several respects: (1) hazards (drought, flood, landslide) were conceptualized as 'moderating variables (MVs)' for a causal chain that is actually mediation (IV -> MV -> DV), and neither formal moderation (interaction) nor mediation models were estimated; (2) separate unadjusted bivariate linear regressions were run on questionnaire perception scores without multivariable controls or adjustment for clustering within the three municipalities; (3) extreme bivariate R2 values (0.80-0.93 in Table 5) reflect unaddressed common-method variance/collinearity; and (4) missing daily temperature records (5-10%) were handled via mean substitution, which artificially compresses variance.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High methodological concern under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies (2 'Yes' items on sample inclusion criteria and setting/subject description; 6 'No' items on exposure validity, objective condition measurement, confounder identification, confounder adjustment, outcome validity, and statistical analysis). Although the study transparently describes its three Nepalese municipalities, randomly samples 103 of 138 WASH schemes constructed during 2011-2021, pilot-tested its instrument, and corroborates broad municipal warming and drying trends using 30-year DHM weather station records, its analytical claims rest on unadjusted bivariate linear regressions linking retrospective perceptions of climate and hazards to self-reported WASH system degradation from the same unblinded WUSC and caretaker respondents. No physical spring discharge or water-quality measurements were collected, confounding factors (such as physiographic zone, scheme age, road construction, and maintenance governance) were not controlled for, mediating pathways were mislabeled as moderation and analyzed piecemeal without accounting for municipal clustering, and purposive respondent eligibility rules produced a heavily male respondent pool (88% of WUSCs and 97% of caretakers).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional quantitative survey of 103 community-managed WASH systems (103 WUSC representatives and 103 caretakers) corroborated by descriptive 30-year meteorological station trend analysis (1994-2024)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 2 Materials and Methods, including Section 2.1 Study area, Section 2.2 Secondary data, Section 2.3 Methodology (Conceptual framework Figure 2, Questionnaire design 2.3.1, Sample size 2.3.2 & Table 1, Hazards 2.3.3, Functionality and FIETS sustainability 2.3.4 & Table 2), and Section 2.4 Data analysis (PDF Pages 2-6); Section 3 Results and Discussion, including Table 3, Table 4, Figure 3, Table 5, Table 6, Figure 4, and Figure 5 (PDF Pages 6-11); Ethics and Data Availability Statements (PDF Page 12).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical design is a cross-sectional quantitative questionnaire survey (fielded January-February 2024 across 103 community-managed WASH systems) using linear regression to examine associations between perceived climate changes, climate hazards, and WASH system impacts, alongside descriptive FIETS sustainability scoring and corroborative station-level climate trend plots. Because there is no experimental randomization, no non-randomized intervention/comparator arm (precluding ROBINS-I), and no qualitative analytical component (precluding CASP and MMAT), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool.
